issues.legal_issue: An agreement to sell does not itself create an interest in or charge over immovable property capable of being transferred as a mortgage.

An intended security created by depositing documents that do not convey title may constitute an equitable mortgage or charge, notwithstanding the absence of a mortgage under Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act.
An equitable mortgage or charge created by deposit of documents is enforceable only against the parties and does not bind a subsequent mortgagee without notice.

A prior equitable mortgage may be postponed to a subsequent mortgage under Section 78 of the Transfer of Property Act where the prior mortgagee’s fraud, misrepresentation, or gross neglect induced the subsequent advance.
A mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Indian law is a legal mortgage, distinct from an equitable mortgage under English law.

A later legal mortgage created by deposit of the requisite title deeds takes priority over an earlier equitable mortgage where the earlier mortgagee failed to disclose its security to the later mortgagee.
